title: Prefrontal Cortex in Trauma
subtitle: Appraisal, inhibition and flexible control
altText: Chalkboard-style clinical neuroscience diagram illustrating prefrontal cortex in trauma across threat, memory, regulation and treatment systems.
learningObjectives: Explain prefrontal cortex in trauma in clinically accurate language.
Distinguish established findings from theoretical or mixed claims in prefrontal cortex in trauma.
Identify one limitation or safety implication relevant to prefrontal cortex in trauma.

sections.explainSimply: Prefrontal systems help evaluate context, inhibit habitual responses and choose actions.
sections.explainLikePsychologist: Under high arousal, top-down control may become less efficient, especially when cues resemble prior threat.
sections.advancedClinicalDetail: Medial and lateral prefrontal regions interact with amygdala, hippocampus and salience networks; simple “offline cortex” explanations overstate the evidence.
sections.thinkOfItLike: Think of prefrontal cortex in trauma as one part of a dynamic safety-and-learning system rather than a single switch.
sections.whyPsychologistsCare: Psychologists need prefrontal cortex in trauma to connect symptoms with learning, context, risk and treatment choice without reducing the person to a brain scan.
sections.whenItGoesWrong: Reduced control during threat is state-dependent, not evidence of permanent loss.
sections.clinicalPearl: Clinical pearl: use prefrontal cortex in trauma to sharpen formulation, not to replace phenomenology or outcome measurement.
sections.practicalExample: A clinician uses prefrontal cortex in trauma to formulate triggers, state shifts, avoidance and functional impact, then monitors whether intervention improves daily life rather than relying on presumed neural change.
sections.limitationsCautions: Reduced control during threat is state-dependent, not evidence of permanent loss. Evidence classification: established network role.
